title: Giving openly is good. Giving secretly to the poor is better.
subtitle: So hidden your left hand does not know
then: Ibn Kathir says concealing charity is better because {idea}it protects you from showing off{/idea}, though open giving is better when others will copy it. Among the seven shaded on the Day is {reward}one who gives so secretly that his left hand does not know what his right gave{/reward}.
now: The bank transfer with no reference name. The envelope slipped under a neighbor's door. The bill quietly paid at the counter for the family behind you. {reward}No one claps.{/reward} That is the point.
old: If no one knows I gave, it does not inspire anyone.
new: Open giving has its place, but my secret gifts protect my heart and reach Allah directly.

title: Guiding them is not your job. Your giving is for you.
subtitle: Kindness to those who do not share your faith
then: Ibn Abbas said the Companions {trap}disliked giving charity to their polytheist relatives{/trap}, until this verse came. Ata said you will not be asked about the receiver. The Prophet ﷺ told of a man who unknowingly gave to a thief, a rich man, and an adulteress; he was told {reward}your charity was accepted{/reward}, perhaps it would change them.
now: Your uncle who mocks your faith is struggling with rent. The neighbor of another religion just lost her job. {idea}You are not their judge, and you do not control their hearts.{/idea} Help them for Allah's sake.
old: My charity should only go to people who deserve it.
new: Guidance belongs to Allah; my job is to give sincerely, and the reward is mine.
try: Do one kind, practical thing for a relative or neighbor you disagree with.

title: The neediest are often the ones too dignified to ask.
subtitle: Look for the poor who look fine
then: These were {idea}emigrants in Madinah who had left everything{/idea} and could not travel to earn. The ignorant {trap}thought them rich because of their restraint{/trap}. The Prophet ﷺ said the truly needy is not the one turned away by a date or two, but {idea}the one who has not enough, whom no one notices, and who asks no one{/idea}.
now: The colleague who always says she is fine but brings no lunch. The student who never joins the group meals. The single dad who keeps quiet. {idea}Look again.{/idea} Find a way to give that does not cost them their dignity.
old: If someone needed help, they would ask for it.
new: The people most in need are often silent, and I should look for them.
try: Think of one person who might be quietly struggling. Find a gentle way to help.

title: Night and day, secret and open: giving as a way of life.
subtitle: Generosity in every season
then: This verse closes the long passage on charity with a portrait: people who give {reward}by night and by day, secretly and publicly{/reward}. Not one big donation, but a life. Their reward is with their Lord, and {idea}no fear or grief{/idea} touches them.
now: You give generously in the last ten nights of Ramadan, then the rest of the year it stops. {idea}What if giving were part of your Tuesday?{/idea} A small regular amount, at any hour, in any mood.
old: Charity is something I do at special times.
new: Giving can be the rhythm of my ordinary days and nights.
try: Set up a small, regular donation today, even a tiny one.

title: They said trade and riba are the same. Allah drew the line.
subtitle: Profiting from another's need versus fair exchange
then: This passage follows the verses on charity, as Ibn Kathir notes: {reward}the givers{/reward} are followed by {trap}those who take people's money unjustly{/trap}. The argument, trade is just like riba, is answered: Allah permitted one and forbade the other. He knows what harms His servants and is {idea}more merciful to them than a mother to her infant{/idea}. Whoever stops, the past is with Allah.
now: Being sure every deal is fair can feel complicated. {idea}Notice the heart of it: does my gain come from someone else's desperation?{/idea} Umar himself said some types of riba were not clear to him. Ask people of knowledge, and take the door the verse leaves open.
old: Money is money; how it grows is just business.
new: How my money grows matters to Allah, and there is always a way back for whoever turns.
try: Look at one of your financial dealings honestly, and ask someone knowledgeable one question about it.

title: Allah drains what riba gathers and grows what charity gives.
subtitle: The hidden arithmetic of money
then: Ibn Mas'ud said riba {trap}ends up with less, even if it was a lot{/trap}. The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever gives even a date from honest earnings, {reward}Allah takes it in His right hand and raises it, as one raises a foal, until it is like a mountain{/reward}.
now: The account keeps growing, but somehow there is never any peace in the house. Meanwhile the family who give from a small income always seem to have enough. {idea}Barakah does not show up on a statement.{/idea}
old: Giving shrinks my money and clever deals make it grow.
new: Allah removes the blessing from unjust gain and grows a single honest date into a mountain.
try: Give the value of a date from honest money today and picture it growing.

title: Faith, good deeds, prayer, zakah: and then no fear.
subtitle: The steady life set beside the anxious chase
then: Between the verses on riba, Allah sets a contrast. Ibn Kathir says the riba-taker is {trap}not satisfied with the pure provision Allah gave{/trap}. Then come those who believe, are kind to creation, pray and give: {reward}their reward is with their Lord, no fear, no grief{/reward}.
now: You lie awake doing sums, chasing the next side hustle, refreshing the crypto app. {idea}The verse offers a different kind of security.{/idea} Pray on time, give what is due, be kind. Let that be the floor under you.
old: I will feel safe once I have enough money.
new: Faith, prayer and giving are the real safety net, here and on the Day.
try: Check that your zakah or regular giving is up to date, and pray your next prayer on time.

title: Let go of what is still owed in riba, if you believe.
subtitle: Walking away from money you were counting on
then: Zayd bin Aslam and others said Thaqif demanded old riba from Banu al-Mughirah after both became Muslim. Banu al-Mughirah said: {idea}we do not pay riba in Islam{/idea}. The governor of Makkah wrote to the Prophet ﷺ, and this verse came. They said: {reward}we repent to Allah and abandon what is left{/reward}.
now: Money you were promised, money you had already planned to spend. {trap}Letting it go feels like losing.{/trap} The verse asks for taqwa exactly there, at the point where it costs you something real.
old: Giving up money I am entitled to is just foolish.
new: Leaving unjust gain behind for Allah is what faith looks like when it costs me.
try: Name one gain you suspect is not clean. Ask someone with knowledge how to make it right.

title: Keep your capital. Do no wrong, and suffer no wrong.
subtitle: A fair deal that cuts both ways
then: The warning is the starkest in the passage: {trap}a war from Allah and His Messenger{/trap}. Yet the door stays open: {reward}if you repent, your capital is yours{/reward}. At the Farewell Hajj the Prophet ﷺ cancelled old riba, starting with his own uncle al-Abbas's: {idea}you take back your capital, wronging no one and not wronged{/idea}.
now: You are afraid that turning back means losing everything you built. {reward}It does not.{/reward} The verse protects you as well as the other person: you keep what is fairly yours. Repentance is not ruin.
old: If I try to fix this, I will lose everything.
new: Allah lets me keep what is fairly mine; only the injustice has to go.
try: Write down one step you could take this month toward cleaner money.
